# Puṇṇanadījātaka (Ja 214)

**ID:** Ja 214

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Puṇṇanadījātaka* (Ja 214), translated as "Who Drinks When the River’s Full," is a birth story belonging to the canonical Pali Jātaka collection. In the commentary's framing narrative (*nidāna*), the Buddha relates the tale while residing at Jetavana, prompted by a discussion in the Dhamma hall concerning his supreme perfection of wisdom (*paññāpāramī*) and penetrative insight [Fausböll 1879]. The verse and story are anchored by the opening phrase *puṇṇaṁ nadiṁ* ("a river that is full") [Fausböll 1879; Fausböll 1891].

At the conclusion of the tale (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies the royal chaplain (*purohita*) of the past as the Bodhisatta himself, and the king as his disciple Ānanda [Fausböll 1879]. The *Puṇṇanadījātaka* is also referenced elsewhere in the Pali commentary, notably in the fifth volume of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā*, where its opening line is quoted as an exemplary demonstration of the preeminence of wisdom's power (*paññābala*) over all other strengths [Fausböll 1891].
